# Existence of a Minimal Uncountable Well-Ordered Set without the Axiom of Choice

We will prove the existence of an uncountable well-ordered set $\Omega$ such that every proper initial segment of $\Omega$ is countable.

Let $A$ be the set of all pairs $(S, R)$ such that $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $R \subseteq S \times S$ is a well-ordering of $S$. Because $S \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ and $R \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N})$, $A$ is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \times \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N})$. By the Axiom of Comprehension, $A$ is a well-defined set in Zermelo-Fraenkel (ZF) set theory without requiring the Axiom of Choice.

We define an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $A$ by declaring $(S_1, R_1) \sim (S_2, R_2)$ if and only if the well-ordered sets $(S_1, R_1)$ and $(S_2, R_2)$ are isomorphic (i.e., there exists a bijective, order-preserving map between them). Let $\Omega = A / \sim$ be the set of equivalence classes. We denote the equivalence class of $(S, R)$ as $[S, R]$.

We define a strict relation $<$ on $\Omega$ as follows: $[S_1, R_1] < [S_2, R_2]$ if and only if $(S_1, R_1)$ is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of $(S_2, R_2)$. This relation is well-defined on equivalence classes because isomorphisms preserve proper initial segments. By a standard theorem of set theory (which requires no Choice), for any two well-ordered sets, either they are isomorphic, or exactly one is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of the other. Thus, $<$ is a strict total order on $\Omega$.

Next, we establish that $(\Omega, <)$ is a well-ordered set. Let $X$ be a non-empty subset of $\Omega$. We must show that $X$ has a least element. Since $X$ is non-empty, we can fix some $\alpha = [S, R] \in X$ (this is existential instantiation, requiring no Axiom of Choice). If $\alpha$ is the least element of $X$, we are done. Otherwise, the set $Y = \{ \beta \in X \mid \beta < \alpha \}$ is non-empty. For each $x \in S$, let $S_x = \{ y \in S \mid y R x \text{ and } y \neq x \}$ be the proper initial segment of $S$ determined by $x$, equipped with the restricted well-ordering $R_x = R \cap (S_x \times S_x)$. Since any proper initial segment of $(S, R)$ is isomorphic to $(S_x, R_x)$ for a unique $x \in S$, the map $x \mapsto [S_x, R_x]$ is a bijection from $S$ to the set of all elements $\gamma \in \Omega$ such that $\gamma < \alpha$. Let $Z = \{ x \in S \mid [S_x, R_x] \in Y \}$. Since $Y$ is non-empty, $Z$ is a non-empty subset of $S$. Because $R$ well-orders $S$, $Z$ has a least element $z_0$ with respect to $R$. Then $[S_{z_0}, R_{z_0}]$ is the least element of $Y$. Furthermore, since all elements in $X \setminus Y$ are greater than or equal to $\alpha$ (which in turn is strictly greater than $[S_{z_0}, R_{z_0}]$), $[S_{z_0}, R_{z_0}]$ is consequently the least element of $X$. Therefore, $(\Omega, <)$ is a well-ordered set.

Now we show that every proper initial segment of $\Omega$ is countable. Let $\alpha = [S, R] \in \Omega$. The proper initial segment of $\Omega$ determined by $\alpha$ is $I_\alpha = \{ \beta \in \Omega \mid \beta < \alpha \}$. As demonstrated above, the map $x \mapsto [S_x, R_x]$ is a bijection from $S$ to $I_\alpha$. Since $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, $S$ is countable. Because $I_\alpha$ is in bijection with a subset of the natural numbers, $I_\alpha$ itself is countable.

Finally, we show that $\Omega$ is uncountable. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $\Omega$ is countable. Since $(\Omega, <)$ is a well-ordered countable set, there exists an injective function $f: \Omega \to \mathbb{N}$. We can define a subset $S^* = f(\Omega) \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and a well-ordering $R^*$ on $S^*$ by $x R^* y \iff f^{-1}(x) < f^{-1}(y)$. Thus, $(\Omega, <)$ is isomorphic to $(S^*, R^*)$. Consequently, $(S^*, R^*) \in A$, and it defines an equivalence class $\alpha^* = [S^*, R^*] \in \Omega$. Since $\alpha^* \in \Omega$, the proper initial segment $I_{\alpha^*}$ is exactly the set of equivalence classes corresponding to all proper initial segments of $(S^*, R^*)$. This means $I_{\alpha^*}$ is isomorphic to $(S^*, R^*)$. However, since $(\Omega, <)$ is isomorphic to $(S^*, R^*)$, this implies that the well-ordered set $(\Omega, <)$ is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of itself ($I_{\alpha^*}$). This is a contradiction, as no well-ordered set is isomorphic to a proper initial segment of itself. 

Therefore, $\Omega$ must be uncountable. Since $\Omega$ is an uncountable well-ordered set such that every proper initial segment is countable, it serves as a minimal uncountable well-ordered set (any well-ordered set strictly smaller than it is isomorphic to a proper initial segment, and is therefore countable).
